plugin.description: Thirty-nine independently usable agent skills for project writing, product narrative, developer adoption, commercial research and consistent project meaning.
plugin.short_description: Project writing, architecture and product skills
plugin.long_description: Geekist's 13 authored skills help with project language, architecture, tasks, reports, technical docs, UX copy, product communication and professional outreach. 26 independently usable upstream skills add further options for storytelling, README craft, editing and developer adoption. Choose each skill for the task at hand; combine skills when the work benefits from more than one perspective.
default_prompts: Turn these requirements into an actionable implementation task with acceptance criteria.
Explain this system in a README section for a new contributor.
Review this draft for clarity, flow and consistent terminology.
Clarify the domain terms in this codebase and make a concise glossary.
Write clear UI messages for these product states.
Research this company for credible collaboration or paid-work opportunities.

advance-with-uncertainty.title: Turn unknowns into actionable next steps
advance-with-uncertainty.purpose: Make open questions, missing evidence, pending checks and real blockers clear enough to act on.
advance-with-uncertainty.when_to_use: Use when a request mentions an unknown, assumption, pending check, evidence gap, unverified claim or blocker. Helps turn uncertainty in implementation tasks, pull-request reviews, plans, research notes, reports and handoffs into clear next steps.
advance-with-uncertainty.example_request: Turn this untested adapter decision into bounded next actions and clear completion evidence.
advance-with-uncertainty.expected_result: A precise gap, the next check, the dependent step and the work that can continue.

example.before: Compatibility has not been checked, so the implementation is paused.
example.after: Implement the authorised adapter. Check one local client event before claiming compatibility; the check is still pending.
example.source_facts: The adapter implementation is authorised. Compatibility has not been checked. One local client-event check is required before claiming compatibility.

advance-with-uncertainty.source_basis: This skill implements the Geekist requirement to make evidence gaps actionable. Related decision principles draw on MADR. It helps agents describe what remains unresolved while identifying useful next actions, without treating ordinary pending work as a reason to abandon an authorised implementation.
advance-with-uncertainty.activation_description: Use when a task, review, plan, report, handoff or status update contains unknowns, untested assumptions, missing evidence, pending checks or unclear blockers. Turn phrases such as not proven, no evidence, unverified or still pending into the next useful check, the affected decision and work that can continue.

interface.short_description: Turn unknowns into useful next actions
interface.default_prompt: Clarify what is still unknown here, name the next check and show which work can proceed.

backend-slice-architecture.title: Review backend capabilities and boundaries
backend-slice-architecture.purpose: Organise backend code around owned capabilities, clear public APIs and explicit orchestration.
backend-slice-architecture.when_to_use: Use for backend architecture reviews, folder and package placement, module boundaries, public APIs, orchestration, refactoring or incremental migrations.
backend-slice-architecture.example_request: Review this service boundary using the existing backend rules; preserve local naming and propose the smallest migration.
backend-slice-architecture.expected_result: A boundary recommendation tied to the existing rules, code and concrete consequences.

example.before: Put the checkout and stock workflows into a shared helper.
example.after: Keep checkout and stock rules inside their capabilities. Coordinate the cross-capability workflow in the existing application surface.
example.source_facts: Checkout and stock are separate owned capabilities. A workflow coordinates both through the existing application surface.

backend-slice-architecture.source_basis: The backend playbook expresses [@pipewrk](https://github.com/pipewrk)'s capability-first architecture rules. Editorial guidance improves the presentation while retaining the public boundaries and orchestration requirements established by the architecture.
backend-slice-architecture.activation_description: Use when reviewing or changing backend architecture, package or folder structure, service boundaries, module ownership, APIs, cross-capability workflows or shared infrastructure. Helpful requests include where should this code live, what belongs in this module, review this backend structure and how should these services coordinate. Apply the Geekist capability-first rules while preserving the repository's stack and existing decisions.

interface.short_description: Review backend modules, APIs and ownership
interface.default_prompt: Review this backend structure for capability ownership, public APIs and clear orchestration.

establish-project-language.title: Define project terms and shared vocabulary
establish-project-language.purpose: Clarify domain concepts, definitions, naming and the meanings used across code and project content.
establish-project-language.when_to_use: Use for domain terminology, glossary creation, onboarding, naming decisions, conflicting definitions or shared language across code, schemas, tests and documents.
establish-project-language.example_request: Find what eligible means in this project and reconcile the code, decisions and interface wording.
establish-project-language.expected_result: A sourced terminology record with context, accepted meanings, aliases and unresolved differences.

example.before: Ready, approved and eligible all mean the account can proceed.
example.after: Keep the three labels distinct until sources establish their meanings. Record which condition permits the account to proceed.
example.source_facts: The sources use ready, approved and eligible. Their equivalence has not been established, and each may express a different condition.

establish-project-language.source_basis: This skill draws on DDD bounded contexts and SKOS concept distinctions, together with terminology practices from Good Docs. It helps contributors agree on the meanings used within a project so that subsequent documents can refer to the same concepts consistently.
establish-project-language.activation_description: Use when a term is unclear, overloaded or used in conflicting ways; when onboarding to a codebase; when creating a glossary; or when deciding how a new concept should be named. Trace terms through code, schemas, tests, decisions, interfaces and documents, then record the meanings and unresolved differences. Helpful requests include what does this mean here, are these two concepts the same, and make a glossary for this project.

interface.short_description: Clarify domain terms, names and definitions
interface.default_prompt: Map these terms to their meanings in the codebase and identify any conflicts or missing definitions.

frontend-slice-architecture.title: Review frontend features and scene boundaries
frontend-slice-architecture.purpose: Organise frontend code around feature ownership, public APIs and thin scene-level composition.
frontend-slice-architecture.when_to_use: Use for frontend architecture reviews, feature and scene boundaries, component placement, shared UI and hooks, refactoring or incremental migrations.
frontend-slice-architecture.example_request: Review these feature and scene boundaries without changing the framework or underlying frontend rules.
frontend-slice-architecture.expected_result: A targeted recommendation preserving feature ownership, public surfaces and scene composition.

example.before: The shared button should own the checkout workflow state.
example.after: Keep checkout workflow state in its feature. Let the scene compose the feature with shared UI primitives.
example.source_facts: Checkout owns its workflow state. The shared button is a UI primitive, and scenes compose features.

frontend-slice-architecture.source_basis: The frontend playbook expresses [@pipewrk](https://github.com/pipewrk)'s feature-first architecture rules. Its guidance clarifies ownership and shared-component boundaries without changing the underlying engineering decisions.
frontend-slice-architecture.activation_description: Use when reviewing or changing frontend architecture, feature and folder structure, scene composition, component ownership, shared UI or hooks. Helpful requests include where should this component live, is this feature boundary clear, review this screen architecture and what belongs in a shared component. Apply the Geekist feature-first rules while preserving the project's framework and existing decisions.

interface.short_description: Review frontend features, scenes and UI ownership
interface.default_prompt: Review this frontend structure for feature ownership, scene composition and shared UI boundaries.

record-architecture-decisions.title: Write architecture decision records and rationale
record-architecture-decisions.purpose: Explain why a technical option was chosen, what alternatives were considered and what follows from the decision.
record-architecture-decisions.when_to_use: Use for ADRs, technical decision records, decision summaries, design rationale, trade-off notes or explanations of why an option was chosen.
record-architecture-decisions.example_request: Record why we chose a shared queue, including alternatives, the pending latency check and when to reconsider.
record-architecture-decisions.expected_result: A decision record with context, options, outcome, consequences and explicit evidence status.

example.before: The shared queue is the best option and will meet the latency target.
example.after: Choose the shared queue for this prototype. Measure latency before claiming the target is met; record what result would trigger reconsideration.
example.source_facts: The shared queue is chosen for a prototype. Latency has not been measured, so meeting the target is still a pending claim.

record-architecture-decisions.source_basis: MADR informs the decision structure, while source checks preserve the status and authority of the decision. The guidance helps maintainers understand why an approach was selected, particularly after the original participants have moved on and the meeting that settled the matter has become a distant organisational legend.
record-architecture-decisions.activation_description: Use when recording or explaining an architecture or technical decision: ADRs, decision notes, accepted options, trade-offs, alternatives, consequences or reconsideration criteria. Also use when someone asks why a design was chosen or wants the decision captured for future contributors. The result can be formal or lightweight.

interface.short_description: Record decisions, trade-offs and consequences
interface.default_prompt: Record why we chose this approach, the alternatives, consequences and what would make us reconsider.

review-project-language.title: Edit, polish and improve project writing
review-project-language.purpose: Improve clarity, flow, voice and consistency in drafts, READMEs, reports, tasks and messages.
review-project-language.when_to_use: Use for editing, proofreading, polishing, rewriting, tightening or reviewing prose, including READMEs, reports, research findings, tasks and messages.
review-project-language.example_request: Review this task, decision and announcement for consistent meanings and explain every consequential edit.
review-project-language.expected_result: Located findings or an authorised revision that preserves meanings, constraints and source claims.

example.before: Improve the eligibility coverage signal across the activation surface.
example.after: Explain what eligibility and coverage mean here, then name the behaviour that should change. Keep eligibility and coverage distinct.
example.source_facts: Eligibility and coverage are distinct project concepts. Their definitions and the intended behaviour need to be established before rewriting the requirement.

review-project-language.source_basis: This skill combines document-first editing with source-integrity checks. It also provides for inspectable revisions where the consequences of an editorial change warrant explanation. Deliberate authorial voice is preserved rather than automatically normalised.
review-project-language.activation_description: Use when someone asks to edit, review, proofread, tighten, polish, rewrite or improve prose. Works with drafts, READMEs, reports, research findings, implementation tasks, messages and documents, including a finishing pass after another skill has drafted them. Preserve the author's meaning and deliberate voice while improving clarity, flow, terminology and navigation.

interface.short_description: Polish drafts, docs, reports and messages
interface.default_prompt: Improve this draft's clarity and flow while preserving its meaning, details and voice.

write-implementation-tasks.title: Turn requirements into clear implementation tasks
write-implementation-tasks.purpose: Translate goals and decisions into work with observable outcomes, acceptance criteria and useful handoffs.
write-implementation-tasks.when_to_use: Use to create or revise tickets, implementation tasks, acceptance criteria, Gherkin scenarios, subtasks, plans, remediation work or worker handoffs.
write-implementation-tasks.example_request: Write a task for members to export their own bookings; keep the access restriction and include failure cases.
write-implementation-tasks.expected_result: A task with observable behaviour, acceptance criteria, validation and precise dependencies.

example.before: Improve export support and validate permissions.
example.after: Let members export their own bookings. Reject exports of another member’s bookings and verify both outcomes.
example.source_facts: Members may export their own bookings. They may not export another member’s bookings.

write-implementation-tasks.source_basis: Goal-oriented task structure is combined with source-preserving editing practices informed by Humanizer and Plain Writing. The skill helps agents describe work in terms an engineer can act upon, while retaining the constraints that determine whether the result is acceptable.
write-implementation-tasks.activation_description: Use when turning a request, decision, defect, feature, research result or remediation finding into actionable work. Covers implementation tasks, tickets, GitHub issues, acceptance criteria, Gherkin scenarios, subtasks, execution plans, worker briefs, handoffs and follow-up actions. Make the expected behaviour, ownership, dependencies and validation clear enough for another person or agent to act.

interface.short_description: Turn requirements into actionable tasks
interface.default_prompt: Turn this outcome into an implementation task with observable behaviour and acceptance criteria.

write-interface-content.title: Write UI copy and UX microcopy
write-interface-content.purpose: Write labels, messages and product interface text that reflect real behaviour and help people act.
write-interface-content.when_to_use: Use for UX writing and in-product language: UI labels, buttons, forms, errors, empty states, progress, onboarding and notifications.
write-interface-content.example_request: Write the interrupted-export message from the state contract and explain that the download is still in progress.
write-interface-content.expected_result: State-accurate interface wording, consistent action names and useful recovery.

example.before: Export success: processing incomplete.
example.after: Your export stopped before completion. Try again.
example.source_facts: The export stopped before completion. The product supports trying again.

write-interface-content.source_basis: The guidance draws on Atlassian's state-aware content practices. It encourages wording that reflects application behaviour and provides useful recovery information, especially where a generic error message would leave the user wondering what the application expects them to do.
write-interface-content.activation_description: Use when writing or reviewing UX copy, microcopy or text inside an app or website: buttons, labels, forms, field hints, validation, errors, empty and loading states, progress, success messages, dashboards, onboarding, tooltips and notifications. Ground each message in what the product actually does and make the next action clear.

interface.short_description: Write clear labels, errors and product messages
interface.default_prompt: Write the UI copy for these states so people understand what happened and what they can do.

write-marketing-content.title: Write product positioning and launch copy
write-marketing-content.purpose: Explain why a product matters to its audience through clear positioning, supported claims and memorable copy.
write-marketing-content.when_to_use: Use for product positioning, product and feature descriptions, README openings, landing pages, portfolio stories, launch copy, newsletters and social posts.
write-marketing-content.example_request: Announce booking exports for members; preserve that background scheduling has not shipped.
write-marketing-content.expected_result: Customer-facing value grounded in actual behaviour, with stronger claims separated for validation.

example.before: Automatically export all your bookings every day.
example.after: Download your bookings when you need them.
example.source_facts: Members can download bookings on demand. Automatic daily scheduling has not shipped.

write-marketing-content.source_basis: This skill connects audience needs to supported product value, incorporating factual checks and voice-sensitive editing informed by Humanizer and Plain Language Editor. The resulting copy should be engaging while remaining accountable to actual product behaviour.
write-marketing-content.activation_description: Use when writing or improving product descriptions, value propositions, product positioning, README introductions, home or landing pages, portfolio narratives, launch announcements, newsletters or social posts. Also use when asked to make a product sound clearer, more compelling, interesting or memorable. Match the audience and support every product claim with source facts.

interface.short_description: Position products and write compelling copy
interface.default_prompt: Explain why this product matters to its audience using only the facts and proof we have.

write-project-content.title: Write project reports, summaries and updates
write-project-content.purpose: Turn project information into useful prose without forcing it into a document template.
write-project-content.when_to_use: Use for project reports, research findings, meeting notes, project briefs, progress updates, postmortems, status summaries and written explanations.
write-project-content.example_request: Write up these investigation findings for the team. Keep observations, conclusions and next steps distinct.
write-project-content.expected_result: A source-faithful, readable report organised for its reader, without unnecessary template sections.

example.before: Investigation completed, several approaches evaluated and a final determination is forthcoming.
example.after: We examined three approaches. Two meet the current requirements; the third needs a capacity test. We can choose between the first two now.
example.source_facts: Three approaches were examined. Two meet current requirements. The third requires a capacity test. No final approach has been chosen.

write-project-content.source_basis: This skill uses Geekist's shared writing conventions for reports, summaries and other general prose when no specialist is a better match. It also supports explicit workflow selection without imposing a universal process.
write-project-content.activation_description: Use for general project writing whenever a request involves writing up, summarising, explaining or organising project information. Covers research notes, investigation findings, reports, meeting notes, project briefs, progress updates, postmortems, status summaries, technical context and other substantive prose. Choose a useful structure for the reader and combine with a specialist when that improves the result.

interface.short_description: Write reports, notes, summaries and updates
interface.default_prompt: Write this up for the team as a clear report with findings, decisions and next steps.

write-technical-documentation.title: Explain systems and write developer docs
write-technical-documentation.purpose: Help technical and non-technical readers understand how a system works and how to use it.
write-technical-documentation.when_to_use: Use to explain systems, APIs, integrations, codebases, architecture and technical findings in READMEs, guides, tutorials, references or onboarding docs.
write-technical-documentation.example_request: Explain the export flow so a marketing reader can find its purpose and an engineer can find the access contract.
write-technical-documentation.expected_result: A purpose-led document with explained terms, visible constraints and routes to exact technical detail.

example.before: The export orchestration materialises capability DTOs through the adapter.
example.after: The export prepares a file of the member’s bookings. Link the access rules and data contract where engineers need the exact details.
example.source_facts: The export prepares a file of the member’s bookings. Access rules and an exact data contract are available to link.

write-technical-documentation.source_basis: Diátaxis informs the organisation of documentation around reader purposes, supported by Good Docs and relevant arc42 architecture views. Editorial checks preserve technical contracts while improving the explanations around them.
write-technical-documentation.activation_description: Use when someone asks to explain a codebase, system, API, integration, architecture or technical behaviour. Covers README files, developer onboarding, guides, tutorials, how-to material, architecture overviews, API references, technical specifications, research write-ups and spike findings. Organise detail around what the reader needs to understand or do.

interface.short_description: Explain systems, APIs and developer workflows
interface.default_prompt: Explain how this system works for its intended reader and point to the useful technical details.

interface.short_description: Research companies, prospects and opportunities
interface.default_prompt: Research this company and identify credible opportunities and conversation angles from current evidence.

research-outreach-opportunities.title: Research companies and commercial opportunities
research-outreach-opportunities.purpose: Find credible reasons to contact, collaborate with or offer useful work to a person or company.
research-outreach-opportunities.when_to_use: Use for company and prospect research, founder research, paid-work opportunities, collaboration ideas, commercial discovery or a suspected content or engineering gap.
research-outreach-opportunities.example_request: We thought this developer tool needed better documentation. Investigate whether that remains true and what other opportunities its customer implementations suggest.
research-outreach-opportunities.expected_result: Current evidence, significant discoveries, revised commercial interpretations and a considered outreach-readiness recommendation.

example.source_facts: A company's old documentation is limited. Newer official documentation now covers the SDK thoroughly. An independent customer implementation illustrates a richer product use case.
example.before: Their developer documentation is poor. Pitch an SDK writing package.
example.after: The current SDK documentation addresses the original gap. The customer implementation suggests an alternative: an engineering-led case study explaining the real integration. This is a conversation angle, not an existing commission.

research-outreach-opportunities.source_basis: Geekist's evidence-led commercial discovery method challenges the initial opportunity hypothesis, distinguishes relationship history from current business evidence, and separates investigation from workflow-specific selection, schemas and sending.
research-outreach-opportunities.activation_description: Use for company, account, prospect, founder or LinkedIn research; commercial opportunity discovery; paid-work and partnership exploration; or investigating a possible content, documentation or engineering gap. Check current first-party and independent evidence alongside known CRM history, then prepare findings and useful conversation angles for personalised outreach.

interface.short_description: Write individual emails, DMs and follow-ups
interface.default_prompt: Draft a natural message to this person using the real context and the author's voice.

write-outreach.title: Write individual professional outreach
write-outreach.purpose: Compose one-to-one professional messages that sound like their author and reflect the real relationship.
write-outreach.when_to_use: Use to write or revise individual professional emails, LinkedIn messages, pitches, introductions, referrals, reconnections and follow-ups.
write-outreach.example_request: Use the research and our earlier conversation to write a personal email to the founder that reflects the real reason for reaching out.
write-outreach.expected_result: A recipient-specific message grounded in real discoveries and relationship context, without invented familiarity, compulsory calls to action or generic sales scaffolding.

example.source_facts: An established contact has previously discussed developer integrations with the author. A recent independent example demonstrates a product capability. The author has not personally tested the integration.
example.before: Hello, I am impressed by your innovative platform. I recently tested your solution and would love to pick your brain about synergy.
example.after: That integration we discussed came to mind when I saw a customer using the shared-session API in a classroom app. Interesting how far beyond browser demos it goes. Have you seen other teams take it in that direction?

write-outreach.source_basis: Adapts Anthropic Outreach Composer and Mangosteen POV alongside Geekist's writing principles. Emphasises relationship history, evidence-led observations, first-person truth, and transferable editorial lessons from authorised author corrections.
write-outreach.activation_description: Use when drafting, editing or reviewing an email, LinkedIn DM, pitch, introduction, referral request, reconnection or follow-up to one person. Works for founder outreach, freelance and consulting enquiries, recruiting messages and professional relationship-building. Ground the message in what the author knows and wants to say; keep the voice natural and the ask appropriate.

readme-craft.title: Readme Craft
readme-craft.purpose: Shape a clear, visual GitHub README that guides readers from first impression to first use.
readme-craft.when_to_use: Generate and improve README files using a 3-tier layout strategy, GitHub-native formatting patterns, badge guidance, and a state-driven workflow. Use when the user says "write a README", "generate a README", "create a README", "improve this README", "review my README", "make my README better", "add badges", or "fix my README layout". For logo generation and comparison screenshots, Node.js 18+ and the npm packages listed in package.json power the bundled scripts; scripts/setup.sh installs those packages.

readme-craft.expected_result: An output shaped by the complete upstream instructions, source material and the task at hand.

example.before: The product has features and should be easier to understand.
example.after: Use the skill's complete instructions to shape a specific, source-faithful result for its intended reader.
example.source_facts: Illustrative example; this entry records source and package review.

portfolio-positioning.title: Portfolio Positioning

bespoke.title: Bespoke
bespoke.purpose: Refine writing in the author's own voice.
bespoke.when_to_use: Act as Bespoke, a content refiner that builds writing from a specific person's real voice instead of generic prose. Use for LinkedIn posts, X/Threads, Substack articles, emails, or Slack messages when the person wants their own personality in the writing, says "write in my voice," "humanize this," "make this sound like me," or hasn't defined a voice yet. Also usable as a file-mode or embedded-mode rewriter (Section 10). Opens with a short intake (Voice, Platform/Task, Audience, Intention) and asks only for what's missing; Voice is an explicit own-style-or-default choice, and own style requires a real writing sample of at least 100 words, not adjectives. Grounded in stylometric voice-fingerprinting, plain-style diagnostics (five pattern clusters covering promotional inflation, hedging, and mechanical uniformity alongside Orwell's four faults), formulaic-language research, and forensic content-analysis criteria for genuine versus fabricated detail, not a fixed list of banned phrases.
